metadata.title: Rent and Shared-Resource Costs by Usage
metadata.description: Allocate a shared rent or expense according to each partner’s time, occupancy, or equivalent resource use.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Allocate common rent or costs in proportion to the relevant usage measure, such as people or animals × time, or occupancy over successive periods. For different resource types, first convert them to a common equivalent only when the problem supplies a valid equivalence (for example, relative feed consumption); then multiply by duration. Explain why unused periods are not charged to departed users, and verify shares sum to total rent. Ground in solved examples 7–9 and objective patterns 4 and 36.

content.text: Rent and Shared-Resource Costs by Usage: Allocate a shared rent or expense according to each partner’s time, occupancy, or equivalent resource use. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Rent and Shared-Resource Costs by Usage asks you to decide what determines each partner’s share. Allocate a shared rent or expense according to each partner’s time, occupancy, or equivalent resource use. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. Shared costs are assigned according to the relevant amount of use, not automatically by partnership capital. Write the partner names and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

A usage weight can be people×time, animals×time, or an equivalent quantity×time. Convert different resource types only when the problem gives a valid equivalence. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once both are expressed in compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: A grazes 15 cows for 4 months, giving 60 cow-months; C grazes 18 cows for 6 months, giving 108 cow-months. C’s rent share is 108/60 times A’s. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Write the unit of the weight (for example, cow-months) to keep the model meaningful. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. If use occurs in different periods, allocate each interval to the people present then; total assigned rent must equal the bill. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Do not use capital-time weights in a rent problem unless capital is the stated basis; identify the resource that drives the cost. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. For mixed animals, first convert each type to a common feeding equivalent, then multiply by time. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for rent and shared-resource costs by usage without relying on a memorized answer pattern.
